proof:
# Positive depth forces an interior point of a positive-volume fiber

Let P be a finite lattice-convex subset of Z^n, let K_z be nonempty compact
convex subsets of R^d, d>=1, and suppose these are the actual fibers of
C=conv union_z ({z} x K_z). Use the finite measure
mu=sum_z delta_z tensor (1_(K_z) dx), with total mass M>0.
The projection may have arbitrary affine rank.

## Lemma

If the normalized ambient halfspace depth of (z,x) is positive, then K_z
has positive d-volume and x belongs to its ordinary interior in R^d.
In fact any point failing this conclusion lies in a closed ambient
halfspace of mu-mass zero.

## Proof

Put Q=conv(P), and let F be the minimal face of Q containing z. Then
z lies in relint(F). Every face of a polytope is exposed, so choose an affine
functional ell on aff(Q) that is zero on F and strictly negative at every
point of P outside F. If F=Q, take ell=0 and omit all off-face arguments.
Extend affine functionals on aff(Q) to R^n when needed.

If every fiber at an index in P intersect F has zero d-volume, the vertical
halfspace ell(w)>=0 contains (z,x) and has zero mu-mass. When F=Q, all fibers
would have zero volume, contradicting M>0; hence this case always has a
nonzero exposing normal and defines a genuine halfspace.

Otherwise form
C_F=conv union_(w in P intersect F) ({w} x K_w).
One positive-volume fiber and an affine basis of indices in F show that
C_F has nonempty relative interior in aff(F) x R^d. Its fiber at z is K_z,
since C_F subset C and C_F contains the entire specified fiber K_z.

If K_z has empty interior or x is on its boundary, (z,x) is on the relative
boundary of C_F: a relative interior ball would include a d-dimensional
ball in that fiber. The supporting hyperplane theorem supplies a nonzero
normal (a,u) on aff(F) x R^d with

    a.(w-z)+u.(y-x) <= 0       for all (w,y) in C_F.

Its continuous component u is nonzero. Indeed u=0 would give a nonzero
supporting linear functional of F at z in relint(F), which is impossible.
Extend a to R^n.

For every off-face index w, the continuous fiber K_w is bounded and
ell(w)<0. Since there are finitely many such indices, choose T>=0 large
enough that

    a.(w-z)+u.(y-x)+T ell(w) < 0

for all their points. The closed ambient halfspace where this last affine
functional is nonnegative contains (z,x). On each face fiber, ell=0 and the
supporting inequality holds, so its intersection is contained in the
continuous hyperplane u.(y-x)=-a.(w-z). This has zero d-dimensional volume
because u!=0. All off-face fibers are excluded. The cap therefore has
mu-mass zero, as claimed. Its ambient normal is nonzero because u!=0.

## Consequence for a finite critical cap cover

Suppose beta>0 is the maximum normalized depth, and a finite family of
closed nonvertical caps H_j covers S with mu(H_j)<=beta M. If y=(z,x) is a
maximizer, every H_j containing y has both mass beta M and its boundary
through y. Equality of masses follows from the definition of depth.
If y were strictly inside H_j, translate its boundary parallel to itself
until it passes through y. The open ball around x in K_z supplied by the
lemma gives a positive-volume slab removed by this translation. The new
containing cap would have mass below beta M, a contradiction.

The continuous normal vectors of the caps through y have zero in their
convex hull. Otherwise strict separation gives a continuous direction v
with every one of their inner products with v negative. A small displacement
of y in direction v stays inside K_z, leaves all those caps, and stays
outside the other finitely many caps (which did not contain y). This
contradicts coverage. Caratheodory's theorem thus supplies a positively
balanced subfamily of at most d+1 active continuous normals. A minimal
such subfamily is a positive circuit.

This is an attained local balance statement. It gives no quantitative
relation between circuits at different integer fibers, and does not by
itself establish the OC constant.
